say.text: Stage III breast cancer: a 6 cm mass, fixed matted axillary nodes, no distant spread. What is the first treatment?

choices.label: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy to shrink disease first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what must be treated before the knife, when the disease has probably spread beyond the breast. Which treatment acts on the whole body?
Yes. Locally advanced disease gets neoadjuvant chemotherapy first, to shrink fixed nodes and the tumour before any surgery.

choices.label: I know this, skip the worked case

say.text: That choice is not right.
Operating first feels decisive, since the breast is the visible disease. But surgery alone leaves the spread untreated and cannot downstage fixed nodes.

sure_note.text: You were sure that surgery comes first. Recheck what neoadjuvant treatment is for before the next question.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Radiotherapy controls the local field but does not treat the systemic spread that stage III carries, so it cannot open the plan.
Worked case, inflammatory carcinoma. Tumour emboli block the dermal lymphatics of the skin, so the disease is treated as spread-prone from day one.
Step 1: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, to treat the spread and shrink the skin disease.
Step 2: modified radical mastectomy. Breast-conserving surgery is never used.
Step 3: radiotherapy to the chest wall after surgery.
Same team, next patient with inflammatory cancer. Which order is correct?

choices.label: Mastectomy, then adjuvant chemotherapy, then radiotherapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then mastectomy, then radiotherapy
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which step must act on the disease before the operation removes the breast, and which step covers the chest wall afterwards.
Yes. Chemotherapy comes first to treat the spread, mastectomy follows, and radiotherapy covers the chest wall after surgery.
That choice is not right.
Adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery looks like the usual sequence, but it leaves micrometastases untreated during the operation, so downstaging is lost.

sure_note.text: You were sure that surgery comes first. Recheck why inflammatory disease is treated before the operation.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Radiotherapy is the last local step after mastectomy in this disease, so it cannot open the sequence.
62-year-old, postmenopausal, ER-positive early breast cancer. Which hormonal drug is the choice?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where this woman's oestrogen still comes from, now that her ovaries have stopped making most of it.
Yes. After menopause oestrogen comes mainly from peripheral aromatisation, so aromatase inhibitors cut the supply.
That choice is not right.
Tamoxifen is the endocrine drug many people reach for first, but it is the premenopausal choice. Menopausal status changes the drug, not ER status alone.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The qualifier that decides the drug is her menopausal status, not the ER result alone.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Raloxifene is used for bone protection and chemoprevention, not as the standard endocrine treatment of early ER-positive cancer.
36-year-old, premenopausal, ER-positive early breast cancer. Which hormonal drug is the choice?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where this woman's oestrogen still comes from, and what each drug does to that supply or to the receptor.
Yes. Premenopausal ovaries still make oestrogen, so tamoxifen, which blocks the receptor, is the choice.
That choice is not right.
Aromatase inhibitors are the postmenopausal drugs. They cut peripheral oestrogen, but in a premenopausal woman the ovaries keep supplying it.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Recheck which drugs suit which menopausal status, since ER positivity alone does not decide.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Trastuzumab targets HER2 and is not a hormonal drug, so a positive ER result does not make it the endocrine choice.
Which is a recognised adverse effect of tamoxifen?

choices.label: Endometrial atrophy that protects the uterus
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the drug does in the lining of the uterus, not only in the breast.
Yes. Tamoxifen acts differently in the endometrium, so it raises endometrial cancer risk; it also causes thromboembolism.
That choice is not right.
A drug that blocks oestrogen in the breast looks protective everywhere, but in the uterus tamoxifen behaves differently, and the endometrium carries the risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure the anti-oestrogen effect carries into the uterus. Recheck tissue-specific action.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Osteoporosis and fractures are aromatase inhibitor effects, from stopping peripheral oestrogen. They are not the uterine risk asked about.
Tamoxifen versus raloxifene: which statement about the endometrium is correct?

choices.label: Neither drug raises endometrial cancer risk
Raloxifene raises it, tamoxifen does not
Tamoxifen raises endometrial risk, raloxifene does not
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of the two drugs acts as an oestrogen-like agent in the uterus.
Yes. Tamoxifen carries the uterine risk, while raloxifene does not, which is why raloxifene suits chemoprevention after menopause.
That choice is not right.
Many SERMs look alike, so 'neither' is tempting, but the uterine risk is not shared by every drug in this class.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the class effect. Recheck which SERM carries the endometrial risk.

say.text: That choice is not right.
This reverses the tissue action of the two drugs. Check which one raises risk in the uterus.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the reversed tissue action. Recheck the two drugs side by side.

say.text: Which statement about trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is correct?

choices.label: Seen only when given with a taxane
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Compare its heart effect with the anthracycline you know. Does a lifetime dose drive it?
Yes. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is usually reversible and not dose-related, so it is monitored during treatment rather than capped by a lifetime dose.
That choice is not right.
The anthracycline pattern is tempting because both drugs damage the heart, but trastuzumab's cardiac effect does not follow the cumulative pattern.

sure_note.text: You were sure the anthracycline pattern transfers. Recheck the dose and reversibility contrast.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A taxane is part of standard chemotherapy, but trastuzumab's heart risk is its own drug toxicity, not one linked to a taxane.
Which agent causes cumulative, largely irreversible cardiomyopathy?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the chemotherapy drug whose total dose is limited because of the heart.
Yes. Doxorubicin cardiomyopathy is dose-dependent and largely irreversible, which is why its cumulative dose is limited.
That choice is not right.
Trastuzumab is tempting because it is a cardiotoxic breast drug, but its cardiac effect is usually reversible and not dose-related.

sure_note.text: You were sure trastuzumab follows the anthracycline pattern. Recheck the two drugs side by side.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Paclitaxel is a standard chemotherapy taxane. Its toxicity is not the cumulative cardiomyopathy this question describes.
Core biopsy of a mammography-detected area shows classic LCIS, with no invasive component. What is the management?

choices.label: Modified radical mastectomy of that breast
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether classic LCIS is itself an invasive cancer, or a marker that raises risk in both breasts.
Yes. Classic LCIS is a risk marker for invasive cancer in either breast, so it is managed by surveillance and chemoprevention, not surgery.
That choice is not right.
Removing the breast is tempting when the word carcinoma appears, but classic LCIS is a marker of risk, not a cancer that needs mastectomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure in-situ disease is removed. Recheck what classic LCIS predicts.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Chemotherapy treats invasive disease that has spread. Classic LCIS has no invasive component to treat.
A woman has classic LCIS found by chance. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: It is a cancer that needs mastectomy to excise
It raises risk of invasive cancer in either breast
It forms a palpable lump and calcifies on film
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what 'lobular' describes here: a mass that shows on imaging, or a marker of risk seen across the breast.
Yes. Classic LCIS does not form a lump or calcify, and it is a risk marker for invasive cancer in either breast.
That choice is not right.
Treating in-situ disease as a cancer to excise is the reflex, but classic LCIS is managed by surveillance, not mastectomy.

sure_note.text: You were sure the in-situ lesion needs excision. Recheck what classic LCIS is.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Palpable lumps and calcification belong to ductal disease, not to classic LCIS, which does neither.
38-year-old, 1.5 cm core-proven invasive ductal carcinoma, node-negative, no symptoms. What next?

choices.label: No routine metastatic imaging; plan local treatment
Baseline CA 15-3 as a staging test
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask who needs a search for distant spread: early asymptomatic disease, or disease that is locally advanced or causing symptoms.
Yes. Routine metastatic imaging is not needed in early, asymptomatic disease. It is done for locally advanced disease or for symptoms.
That choice is not right.
Bone is the commonest site of spread, so a bone scan feels like routine care, but distant-spread imaging follows stage and symptoms.

sure_note.text: You were sure a scan is routine. Recheck the indications for metastatic work-up.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A tumour marker is not a staging test in early disease, and it does not replace the stage-and-symptom indication.
Patient A has early asymptomatic cancer. Patient B has stage III disease with bone pain. Who needs staging imaging?

choices.label: Patient B only, the locally advanced case
Patient A only, since she is young
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which patient has locally advanced disease or symptoms, the two indications for metastatic work-up?
Yes. Patient B has locally advanced disease and bone pain, so imaging for metastatic spread is indicated. Patient A has neither indication.
That choice is not right.
Routine scans feel thorough for everyone, but early asymptomatic patients do not need the metastatic work-up. Stage and symptoms set the indication.

sure_note.text: You were sure imaging is routine. Recheck the indications, not the habit.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Imaging follows stage and symptoms, so this option images the patient without either indication and misses the one with both.
